title: The machine room
dek: Full desk configurations for 2026, and what to wait for in 2027. Computers from a browser desk to an AI video studio, the drives and docks around them, and the pads, pedals and lights an agent can learn to press.
heroAlt: Pixel-dithered specimen sheet of desk hardware: a small desktop box, a tower, a drive, a macro pad, a foot pedal, a key light and a microphone
lede: This started as a disk cleanup. The iMac was full, swapping hard, and the agents were winning.
intro: So we asked the obvious question: what is the next machine, and what goes around it? The answer in 2026 is less about the chip and more about memory, drives, and the small tools on the desk. Prices moved a lot this year. Memory shortages pushed nearly everything up, from SSDs to GPUs to the Mac mini.

Below: five complete desks with totals, then every part on its own card with a dated price, a direct link, and, where it exists, an “agent handle”: how an AI agent can see or press it. Then the fun part. How the desk becomes modular, what we would ask hardware makers for, and what PointCast might build.
method: Desk review. Prices and specs were checked on makers’ own pages on September 29, 2026, US dollars before tax. Where a maker hid the price we used a major retailer and said so; estimates are labeled. Nobody here has handled most of these products.
disclosure: No paid links. Every link goes straight to the maker or the page we checked. No maker paid for placement or saw this before it published.

baseline.title: A 2024 iMac, out of room.

facts.label: Runs
facts.value: Chrome, Claude, Codex, ChatGPT, agents building sites

notes: The disk refills about 25GB a day: every agent task makes a fresh copy of a website and its build folders. A daily 3:30 AM sweep now clears what can be rebuilt, and we moved Unity and a game launcher out (28GB).
Memory is the real ceiling. With three AI apps, a browser and a couple of builds, 24GB spends its day swapping to disk, which is also why that disk wears out faster.
baseline.verdict: Fine for the browser and cloud AI. Out of memory and drive space for local video.

items.name: MacBook Air 15", M5, 24GB
items.why: The browser-and-AI-apps machine. Cloud models do the heavy lifting, so what you need locally is enough memory for thirty tabs, three agent apps and a dev server. 24GB is the floor we would buy.
items.forWho: Browser, ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, light builds.
items.verdict: The honest answer for most people.

items.name: MacBook Pro 16", M5 Max, 128GB
items.why: A Mac Studio’s brain in a laptop: 40-core GPU, 128GB and 614GB/s of memory bandwidth. Runs large local models and cuts AI video anywhere.
items.forWho: A studio that has to travel.
items.catch: OLED models are rumored for late 2026 to early 2027. If you can wait, a laptop is where waiting pays off.

items.name: Mac mini, M6, 32GB
items.why: Apple’s first 2nm chip, in the cheapest desktop. With 32GB it is a quiet always-on box for agents, builds and small local models.
items.forWho: An always-on agent box under a monitor.
items.verdict: Best value Mac on the page.
items.priceNote: The M6 tops out at 32GB. Base model is $899 with 16GB.

items.name: Mac mini, M5 Pro, 64GB
items.why: Twice the memory and bandwidth of the M6 mini. 64GB runs mid-size local models comfortably next to everything else.
items.forWho: Local models on a budget, plus agent work.

items.name: iMac, M4, 24GB
items.why: The machine this guide was written on. A lovely screen and a fine browser computer, but still on M4, and memory tops out low for AI work.
items.forWho: Families and browser work.

items.name: Mac Studio, M5 Max, 64GB
items.why: The full M5 Max, 40 GPU cores each with a Neural Accelerator and 614GB/s of bandwidth, with 64GB. This is the level above an iMac for AI video editing, upscaling and mid-size local models.
items.forWho: An AI video desk that edits locally and generates in the cloud.

items.name: Mac Studio, M5 Max, 128GB
items.why: Same chip, double the memory and storage. 128GB is where large open video and language models start to fit on a Mac.
items.forWho: Running open video models locally, not just editing.
items.priceNote: $3,799 preset plus $1,600 memory and $500 storage, from Apple’s configurator.

items.name: Mac Studio, M5 Ultra, 256GB
items.why: Two M5 Max dies: 64 GPU cores and 1.2TB/s of bandwidth. 256GB holds very large local models and 8K multi-stream timelines.
items.forWho: A local model lab, or a studio with no cloud bill.
items.verdict: Only if the cloud is the problem.
items.priceNote: $5,499 base plus $4,000 memory and $1,500 storage. The 80-core GPU version starts at $6,799.

items.name: RTX 5090 workstation
items.why: NVIDIA is still where open-source video generation runs fastest: ComfyUI, Wan and Hunyuan-class models on CUDA with 32GB of VRAM.
items.forWho: Generating open-model video locally, every day.
items.verdict: Rent it before you build it.
items.priceNote: Estimate. The card’s MSRP is $1,999 but street price is about $4,200–5,100; we could not verify a builder page.

items.name: NVIDIA DGX Spark
items.why: A small CUDA box with 128GB of unified memory and a 4TB drive. Its bandwidth (273GB/s) is well under an M5 Max, so it is for developing and fine-tuning on CUDA, not raw speed.
items.forWho: CUDA development and fine-tuning at the desk.
items.priceNote: Rose from $3,999 in February 2026 because of memory supply.

items.name: Framework Desktop, 128GB
items.why: AMD’s Ryzen AI Max+ with 128GB of shared memory in a small, repairable box. A cheap way to hold big local models on Linux.
items.forWho: Linux tinkerers running large local models.
items.verdict: Great idea, bad month to buy it.
items.config: Ryzen AI Max+ 395 · 16 cores · 40 graphics cores · 128GB
items.catch: Launched at $1,999; memory prices pushed it to $3,449, and it is sold out. Weak for CUDA-only video tools.

items.name: Rent an RTX 5090
items.why: A 32GB RTX 5090 by the hour. At about a dollar an hour you would need four to five thousand hours before buying one pays off.
items.forWho: Anyone curious about local video generation before spending $6,000.
items.priceNote: Secure Cloud on-demand. An H100 is $3.49/hr; a B200 is $6.79/hr.

items.name: Crucial X10, 4TB
items.why: The cheap fix for a full internal drive. Move the media archive (Downloads, Midjourney sessions, Sora exports) here and the agents get the internal drive back. It is rated 2,100 MB/s on USB 20Gbps, but Macs do not speak that mode, so plan on about 1,000 MB/s. That is plenty for an archive you browse, not edit from.
items.forWho: The archive: finished generations, exports, zips you keep “just in case”.
items.verdict: The one to buy this week.
items.config: 4TB · USB 3.2 Gen 2x2 · ~1,000 MB/s on a Mac
items.catch: SSD prices roughly doubled in the last year. This is still the best dollars-per-terabyte we could verify.

items.name: OWC Envoy Ultra, 4TB
items.why: The only Thunderbolt 5 portable we could verify, and the fastest: past 6,000 MB/s on a Thunderbolt 5 Mac. That speed matters for a working drive you cut video from, not for an archive.
items.forWho: Editing 4K and AI video straight off the drive.
items.verdict: A hot drive for a studio, not a closet.
items.catch: Launched at $599.99; OWC lists it at $1,379.99 today. Sustained writes drop to about 1,700 MB/s once the cache fills.

items.name: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
items.why: A four-bay network drive with a 10-gigabit port, which pairs with the CalDigit dock’s 10GbE. Built-in photo recognition. This is where a household’s media lives once one SSD is not enough.
items.forWho: Everything you never want to lose, shared across machines.
items.verdict: Best value network storage for a media house.
items.priceNote: Hard drives are not included; budget for them separately.

items.name: Backblaze Personal Backup
items.why: Unlimited offsite backup for one computer, including drives plugged into it. The cheapest insurance on this page.
items.forWho: The copy that survives a fire, a theft, or a bad rm.
items.verdict: Turn it on before you buy anything else.
items.priceNote: Also $9 a month. It does not back up a NAS, only drives attached to the Mac.

items.name: CalDigit TS5 Plus
items.why: One cable to the Mac, then 10-gigabit Ethernet, two Thunderbolt 5 ports, ten USB ports, card readers and 140W charging. The 10GbE port is the reason: it makes the NAS feel local.
items.forWho: A desk with a NAS, a display and too many cables.
items.config: TB5 host (up to 120Gb/s) · 2× TB5 · 10GbE · DP 2.1 · SD + microSD · 140W

items.name: OWC Thunderbolt 5 Dock
items.why: Three Thunderbolt 5 ports, 2.5GbE, card readers and 140W for $180 less than the CalDigit.
items.forWho: A desk without a NAS.

items.name: ASUS ProArt PA27JCV
items.why: A 27-inch 5K panel with 99% DCI-P3 and USB-C, for less than half the Studio Display.
items.forWho: Anyone buying a Mac mini or Mac Studio who wants 5K text without the Apple tax.
items.priceNote: Newegg price; launched at $799 and ASUS’s own store page errored.

items.name: LG UltraFine evo 32U990A
items.why: A 32-inch 6K Nano IPS Black panel with Thunderbolt 5. More room for a timeline and a terminal side by side.
items.forWho: Video editors who want a bigger canvas than 27 inches.

items.name: Apple Studio Display (2026)
items.why: Same 27-inch 5K panel as 2022, now with Thunderbolt 5 and a 12MP Center Stage camera. The easy answer with a Mac.
items.forWho: People who want one cable and a camera built in.
items.priceNote: $1,999 with the height-adjustable stand; nano-texture is $300 more.

items.name: Apple Studio Display XDR
items.why: A 27-inch 5K mini-LED at 120Hz and 2,000 nits for HDR. It replaced the Pro Display XDR in March.
items.forWho: Grading HDR video for a living.
items.priceNote: With the height-adjustable stand; $2,899 with a VESA mount.

items.name: CyberPower CP1500PFCLCD
items.why: A 1500VA pure sine wave battery backup. A power blip mid-render or mid-migration costs more than this box.
items.forWho: Any desk running long jobs overnight.
items.verdict: The pick: more watts for less money.

items.name: eero Pro 7, two-pack
items.why: Wi-Fi 7 mesh with two 5GbE ports per unit. Worth it with multi-gig internet; otherwise a cable from the dock does more for moving files.
items.forWho: Houses with multi-gig internet and 6GHz devices.
items.verdict: Skip unless your internet is faster than your Wi-Fi.

items.name: Eagle
items.why: Indexes folders in place and finds images by similarity or meaning without tags, with AI actions for tagging and renaming. It is built for design references, which is what a folder of Midjourney and Sora output really is.
items.forWho: Folders of AI generations and design references.
items.priceNote: Eagle did not show a base price on the pages we could load; 30-day free trial.

items.name: Excire Foto 2027
items.why: Private, on-device search across a large photo archive: objects, faces, text in images, aesthetic ratings and duplicate detection. Nothing uploads.
items.forWho: A big photo archive you want to search without a cloud.

items.name: Codex Micro
items.why: OpenAI’s first branded hardware: a macro pad whose Agent Keys light up with each Codex thread’s state (thinking, running, waiting, done) and turn red on an error. Command keys accept, reject and push to talk; a joystick fires saved workflows; a dial sets reasoning effort.
items.forWho: Codex users who want agent status in their peripheral vision.
items.verdict: The right idea, locked to one agent.
items.config: 13 switches · Agent Keys · joystick · reasoning dial · BT + USB-C
items.priceNote: Price from launch press (July 15, 2026); OpenAI’s page blocked our check.

items.name: Creator Micro 2
items.why: The unbranded sibling you can still buy: the same Agent Keys, push-to-talk and command keys, joystick and reasoning dial. The PRO model adds Bluetooth and a battery.
items.forWho: Anyone who wanted a Codex Micro and missed it.
items.verdict: The one to buy if you want an agent pad today.
items.agentHandle: Codex inside Codex; other apps via Work Louder’s Input app

items.name: Stream Deck +
items.why: Eight LCD keys, four dials and a touch strip. Since Stream Deck 7.4 it ships an official MCP server: you place actions on a virtual “MCP Deck” and an AI assistant can press only those.
items.forWho: The desk where agents and hands share the same buttons.
items.verdict: The best agent-controllable surface you can buy.

items.name: Stream Deck MK.2
items.why: Fifteen LCD keys, the classic. Same software, same MCP server, no dials.
items.forWho: More buttons, fewer knobs.

items.name: Stream Deck Neo
items.why: Eight keys and two touch points for under $100. Enough for accept, reject, talk and a few saved prompts.
items.forWho: A first control surface.

items.name: MX Creative Console
items.why: A keypad with LCD keys plus a wireless dialpad, tuned for creative apps through Logi Options+.
items.forWho: Photo and video apps first, agents second.
items.verdict: Good for Premiere, weaker for agents.

items.name: Keychron Q0 Max
items.why: A metal number pad with a knob that runs open QMK firmware. Any key can send anything, and code on your Mac can talk to it over raw HID.
items.forWho: Tinkerers who want an open pad to program.
items.agentHandle: Open QMK/VIA; raw HID from your own scripts

items.name: Stream Deck Pedal
items.why: Three foot pedals with adjustable tension, run by the Stream Deck app. Put push-to-talk under your foot and your hands stay on the keyboard while you talk to an agent.
items.forWho: Dictating to agents all day.
items.agentHandle: Official MCP server, via the Stream Deck app

items.name: Wispr Flow Pro
items.why: Dictation that works in every app, on Mac, Windows and phones. Talking is faster than typing prompts.
items.forWho: Anyone who writes long prompts.
items.verdict: The default for talking to agents.
items.priceNote: $12 a month billed yearly; free tier available.

items.name: superwhisper Pro
items.why: Hotkey dictation with offline local models, or your own API keys. Your voice can stay on the Mac.
items.forWho: Private, local dictation.
items.priceNote: Price from the site’s own code, not a visible page; free tier available.

items.name: Elgato Key Light
items.why: The standard video-call light, controlled over Wi-Fi from the Elgato app or a Stream Deck.
items.forWho: Video calls and recording yourself.
items.verdict: The best call light, and scriptable.

items.name: Elgato Key Light Neo
items.why: A smaller, cheaper Key Light for a desk monitor.
items.forWho: A single desk and a webcam.

items.name: Philips Hue + Bridge
items.why: The most mature light system to script: a local REST API on the Bridge, Matter support, and several community MCP servers. Make the room turn amber when an agent is waiting on you.
items.forWho: Ambient status for agents across a room.
items.verdict: The light to wire to your agents.
items.agentHandle: Local REST API · Matter · community MCP servers

items.name: Nanoleaf panels
items.why: Wall panels with a documented local API. A good glanceable “board” for agent status.
items.forWho: A wall that shows what the agents are doing.

items.name: Shure MV7+
items.why: USB-C and XLR, voice isolation, tap to mute. A dynamic mic rejects the room, which makes dictation and calls cleaner.
items.forWho: Dictation, calls, podcasts.
items.priceNote: Price from Shure’s page data, not a visible tag.

items.name: RØDE PodMic USB
items.why: A dynamic broadcast mic with USB and XLR for $90 less than the Shure.
items.forWho: The same job on a smaller budget.

items.name: Elgato Facecam
items.why: 1080p60 on a Sony STARVIS sensor with a privacy shutter, controlled from a Stream Deck.
items.forWho: A fixed desk camera.

items.name: Raspberry Pi 5, 16GB
items.why: A tiny always-on computer for a house agent: run the status lights, the TRMNL feed, a local speech model, or an MCP bridge to everything else on this list.
items.forWho: The always-on node that ties the desk together.
items.agentHandle: Linux; run any MCP server on it
items.priceNote: Price listed on raspberrypi.com for the 16GB model; memory prices have pushed it up. The 40-TOPS AI HAT+ 2 is about $130 more.

items.name: TRMNL
items.why: An e-ink dashboard with open firmware, webhooks, private plugins and an API. It shows a daily brief or agent status without another glowing screen.
items.forWho: Passive, glanceable status.

modular.lede: The interesting part is not a faster box. It is the desk turning into small tools an agent can see and press: a key that lights up when a thread needs you, a pedal to talk, a lamp that goes amber when a render finishes, a drive that files itself. Most of the parts exist. They just do not talk to each other yet.

asks.title: Ship an MCP server in the box.
asks.body: Elgato did it for Stream Deck in version 7.4. Every light, pad, drive and camera should arrive with one, so any agent can use it on day one.

asks.title: Show agent state, for any agent.
asks.body: Codex Micro’s Agent Keys (thinking, running, waiting, done, red for error) are the right idea. Make that vocabulary open so Claude Code, Codex and the rest can all light the same key.

asks.title: Stay on the local network.
asks.body: Hue, Nanoleaf and Key Light all answer on the LAN. The desk should keep working when a company’s server goes dark.

asks.title: Let people set the permissions.
asks.body: Stream Deck’s MCP Deck is the model: an agent can press only the buttons you put on its deck. Every device should work that way.

asks.title: Print memory and bandwidth on the box.
asks.body: They decide what models a machine can run. Put them next to the price, not three clicks down.

asks.title: Open firmware, repairable parts.
asks.body: QMK pads, TRMNL’s open firmware, Framework’s swappable boards. Modular only works if you can open it.

build.title: The Agent Light.
build.body: A small open spec and script that maps agent hook events (thinking, waiting on you, done, error) to any light or key on this page. One status vocabulary for every agent.

build.title: A PointCast deck.
build.body: A Stream Deck MCP Deck with town actions: post to Shortwave, open today’s block, ring the bell, check the deploy.

build.title: The desk bus.
build.body: A Raspberry Pi 5 running Home Assistant and MCP bridges, so every part here shows up to an agent as one tool list.

build.title: A TRMNL page.
build.body: The Morning Edition on e-ink, plus the machine’s own vitals: disk free, swap, last night’s sweep.

build.title: The sweep, shared.
build.body: The daily disk-cleanup script that keeps this iMac alive, published as a recipe for anyone running agents on a small drive.

modular.note: These are ideas, not products. Nothing in this section is for sale.

foresight.what: M6 is here, but only in the base Mac mini.
foresight.note: Apple’s first 2nm chip shipped September 22 in the $899 Mac mini. M6 Pro, Max and Ultra are not announced.
Apple lists the 512GB memory option as coming late October.

foresight.what: OLED MacBook Pro with M6 Pro and M6 Max.
foresight.note: Bloomberg reports a thinner, touch-capable OLED redesign, possibly sold above the M5 models rather than replacing them.
TrendForce raised its Q3 PC DRAM forecast to +18–23% and sees Q4 at 0–5%, with server memory tight into 2027. It already shows: DGX Spark +$700, Framework +$1,450, SSDs roughly doubled.
Reported postponed because of GDDR7 shortages. NVIDIA has not announced them.
Leakers point to the second half of 2027, possibly Q4, while NVIDIA feeds data centers first.

waitRule: If your work is waiting on the machine, buy now: memory went up all year and is forecast to stay tight. If you are buying a laptop and can wait, wait for the M6 Pro redesign. Desktops can go now; the next Mac Studio is probably a year or more away.
endnoteTitle: Buy memory, then drives, then buttons.
verdict: For the desk this was written on: the Crucial X10 and Backblaze this week, then a Mac Studio M5 Max with 64GB when the budget is ready. Edit locally, generate in the cloud, rent a 5090 by the hour when curiosity strikes. Add a Stream Deck with its MCP server and a pedal, and let the agents start pressing buttons.
